definition: The eight-point algorithm is an algorithm used in computer vision to estimate the essential matrix or the fundamental matrix related to a stereo camera pair from a set of corresponding image points.
details: It was introduced by Christopher Longuet-Higgins in 1981 for the case of the essential matrix. In theory, this algorithm can be used also for the fundamental matrix, but in practice the normalized eight-point algorithm, described by Richard Hartley in 1997, is better suited for this case. The algorithm's name derives from the fact that it estimates the essential matrix or the fundamental matrix from a set of eight (or more) corresponding image points. However, variations of the algorithm can be used for fewer than eight points.

explainer.lead: The eight-point algorithm uses matching points in two camera views to estimate a matrix that describes their geometric relationship. It gives computer-vision systems a way to work with stereo image pairs.

tiers.eli5: Imagine taking two photos of the same toy from slightly different spots and marking the same eight dots in both photos. The algorithm uses those pairs of dots to work out a mathematical description of how the two views relate. Its name comes from the eight matching points it normally uses.
tiers.practitioner: Provide at least eight corresponding image points and use the algorithm to estimate either the essential matrix or the fundamental matrix for a stereo pair. For practical fundamental-matrix estimation, prefer Hartley's normalized eight-point algorithm; variants can handle fewer than eight points.
tiers.paperLevel: Given eight or more point correspondences from a stereo camera pair, the algorithm estimates the essential matrix E or, in principle, the fundamental matrix F. Christopher Longuet-Higgins introduced it for the essential matrix in 1981. Richard Hartley described the normalized eight-point algorithm in 1997, which is better suited in practice to estimating F; variants can use fewer than eight points.

explainer.example: Two stereo cameras photograph a box, and eight visible corners are matched between the images. The algorithm uses those eight correspondences to estimate a matrix relating the two camera views.
